1:
The opening condition is taken as granted, not questioned. Robertson calls it a condition of the first class, assumed as true, and adds that what is offered in place of merely ascetic rules is an ideal and a goal. Gill says the rising is not called in question but taken for granted, and distinguishes three senses: representatively, when Christ rose as their head; emblematically, in baptism; and spiritually, in conversion. Ellicott renders it ye rose and refers it to baptism, then draws an argument about practice. A sudden passing from death to life, he says, accords more exactly with adult baptism accepted in conscious faith, whereas the later word regeneration, which has the soul pass into a new condition but with only the germ of the new life, answers more closely to the infant baptism that superseded it. He notes besides that the name of Christ, four times repeated, carries the article every time, used emphatically of the Mediator as Prophet, Priest and King.

Calvin reads the exhortation as a weapon in the previous chapter’s argument. Against the fruitless exercises the false teachers urged as though perfection lay in them, the apostle sets the true exercises that become Christians; and when we see what God would have us do, human traditions vanish into smoke. He also anticipates the objection it invites: would you rather men were idle than busy about exercises of some sort? Henry states the same in his own key: though free from the ceremonial law we may not live as we list, but must walk the more closely with God; and his reason for seeking things above is simply that Christ sits there.

At the second verse the range of what is forbidden divides them. Calvin narrows it further than anyone: the earthly things meant are not depraved appetites, nor riches or fields or houses or anything of the present life, but still the ceremonies, which he pictures as entanglements constraining us to creep along the ground — Christ calling us upward while these draw us down. He will not contend with those of another mind, but holds that the argument goes forward step by step, setting traditions about trivial matters against meditation on the heavenly life first. Barnes takes the opposite range, naming wealth, honour and pleasure, houses and lands, scenes of fashion and gaiety. Gill keeps it general: the treasure being above, the heart should be there too.

Two notes refuse to let the command become otherworldliness. Robertson glosses the verb as keep on thinking about, remarks that it does matter what we think and that we are responsible for our thoughts, and denies that we are told never to think of earthly things at all — only that these are not to be our aim, since the Christian must keep his feet on the earth and his head in the heavens, and so help make earth like heaven. Clarke turns it into a rule of exchange: act now in reference to heavenly things as you formerly acted in reference to earthly ones, and the reverse — be as much in earnest for the eternal as you once were for the perishing. Wesley compresses the ground into a clause: Christ, being risen, immediately went to heaven.

Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse not as exhortation but as proof-text, collecting it with the other testimonies to the Son’s sitting at the right hand from the Gospel, from Peter, and from the letters to Rome and Ephesus. Two other blocks at this verse are not about it. Tertullian’s expounds a passage in another epistle about men who preached Christ of envy and strife, arguing that the diversity lay in their tempers and not in their doctrine, since one Christ alone was announced. And the note under Barnes opens with a full analysis of the chapter, numbering its seven divisions, before reaching the words in hand.
3:
Gill takes the death by exclusion, ruling out three senses before allowing a fourth. It is not natural, since they were living in the world; not moral, since they had been quickened out of a death in sins; not legal, since their trespasses were forgiven. What remains is a death to the law, to sin as to its damning power, and to the world by the cross — so that a believer should have no regard to the rudiments of the world or the ordinances of men. Ellicott renders it ye died and takes it in its whole sense at once, both death to sin and death to the visible world. Robertson marks it a definite event; Barnes draws out the comparison, that as Christ became literally dead in the tomb, so we are to be to earthly ambition as if we were dead, and it had no more influence over us than the things of earth had over him in the grave. Calvin reverses the argument, reasoning from the consequent to the antecedent, since no one can rise again with Christ who has not first died with him.

The hidden life is imagined three ways. Robertson makes it a strongbox: the perfect tense has it remaining concealed, locked together with Christ and in God, and no hellish burglar can break that combination. Barnes makes it a treasure laid up in a place of security, and observes that it is not left with us or entrusted to our keeping, since then it might be lost or wrested from us. Clarke turns it back on the heart, since Christ is the treasure and where the treasure is the heart is, so that those whose heart is in him sit in heavenly places already.

Calvin alone asks what the hiddenness is for. It is hidden, he answers, so that we may not murmur when our life, buried under the ignominy of the cross, differs nothing from death, but may wait patiently for the day of revelation; and lest the waiting be painful he offers two securities, that God is faithful and will not deny what has been committed to him, and that the fellowship of Christ brings a greater security still. Wesley says the same shortly, that the real and spiritual life is hidden from the world and laid up in God with him who merited and prepared it, giving us the earnest of it meanwhile.

Ellicott reads the four verses as one structure and says so. The first marks the beginning of the spiritual life, the middle its continuance, the last its close; and he notes the movement from the lower expression to the higher, since it is one thing to say our life is hid with Christ and another that Christ is our life. The whole passage, he concludes, forms a complete and magnificent picture of the spiritual life in Christ, the means of its beginning, the signs of its presence and the hope of its close.

At the appearing the notes are brief and one is memorable. Robertson makes the temporal clause indefinite, whenever Christ is manifested, longed for but wholly uncertain as to time, and adds that not to respond to so high an appeal is to be like the man with the muck-rake. Wesley catches the effect of the syntax: the abruptness of the sentence surrounds us with sudden light. Calvin calls it a choice consolation that the coming of Christ will be the manifestation of our life, and adds how unreasonable is the disposition of a man who refuses to bear up until that day. Gill notes a variant, that some copies read your life for our life, and takes the phrase to mean that it is not so much they that live as Christ that lives in them. Barnes and Clarke both refer the appearing to the day of judgment.
5:
Ellicott calls the command doubly unique and says the text is only half the truth. This is the one place where mortification is enjoined at all, and it does not distinguish the members from the evil of which they are made instruments — whereas Scripture generally does, and we are usually bidden not to kill our members but to turn them into instruments of righteousness. Gill draws the same distinction another way: the members are not those of the natural body but of the body of sin, and what is killed is not the principle of indwelling sin, which remains as long as they are in this tabernacle, but the deeds. Calvin distinguishes two mortifications, the outward already treated and this inward one of the understanding and will, granting that the vices are called members not with strict accuracy but elegantly.

How hard the killing is meant to be, each says his own way. Wesley makes it a slaying with a continued stroke. Henry makes it extermination, killing them as one does weeds or vermin, which spread and destroy all about them, or as one kills an enemy who fights and wounds. Clarke defines the verb as depriving a thing of its power and adds a rule: to gratify a sensual appetite is to give it the food by which it lives, and however the body suffers by excess, the appetite increases with the indulgence — so let reason rule, and never let the beast run away with the man. Robertson notes that the English word is drifting towards putrefaction, and that the metaphor of death pictured in baptism is applied to the actual life of a Christian, who is not to take the opposite extreme of license on the plea that the soul is unaffected by the body.

The last item in the list draws the sharpest comment. Wesley derives the word as the desire of having more, or of anything independent of God, and calls it idolatry directly, since it gives the heart to a creature. Clarke says the covetous man makes his money his god. Chrysostom calls it worse than any other desire and more grievous than the silly weakness about silver he had been rebuking. His note is in fact an apology to a congregation: he knows many were offended by his previous discourse, and asks what he can do when they have heard what the Master enjoined, protesting that he speaks not for authority’s sake but out of pain, and would not violate decency by such subjects were he not compelled to it. Barnes notes only that this vice is always ranked with the rest.

At the wrath Calvin will not fix the tense. The present is often used for the future after the Hebrew idiom, so he leaves the rendering undecided, to suit either the ordinary judgments of God seen daily or the vengeance impending until the last day. He also notices what the sentence does not do: it says the wrath comes upon the disobedient rather than threatening the readers with it, since God would rather we saw his wrath upon the reprobate than felt it in ourselves. Robertson insists that these sins are no matter of indifference, and notes that many old manuscripts lack the clause about the sons of disobedience. Wesley adds that the heathen regarded them lightly.

On the past life two voices make the same distinction. Calvin separates living from walking as power differs from action, and corrects a rendering that referred the phrase to men rather than to the vices. Wesley gives it in nine words: living denotes the inward principle, walking the outward acts. Ellicott has the former condition as the element they lived in, and notes that their own active participation is marked as well. Gill makes sin a road of the sinner’s own choosing, dark and crooked, along which walking means a continued sinning.
8:
Robertson alone sees that one figure governs the passage: clothing, running through four verbs in as many verses — laying aside like old clothes, stripping clean off, putting on, and putting on again — the vices being so many filthy rags. Gill has the same, that they are put off as filthy garments never to be worn again. Henry supplies the moral shape: as appetites were mortified, so now passions; anger and wrath are bad but malice worse, being more rooted and deliberate; and as corrupt principles in the heart must be cut off, so must their product in the tongue. Calvin notes that the second word denotes a more impetuous passionateness than the first. Wesley is startled the warning was needed: what is man until perfect love casts out both fear and sin?

Two terms are contested. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott take the word rendered blasphemy of injurious speech against men rather than God. On the next they part: Barnes makes it lewd discourse and Robertson low and obscene speech, while Ellicott holds the context points to grossness of insult rather than filthiness.

The prohibition of lying is grounded differently in different hands. Robertson renders the imperative as stop lying, or do not make a habit of it. Calvin widens it past calumny to every sort of cunning. Barnes calls it a universal fruit of sin, reigning most widely where the gospel has not come. Clarke brings it to the market, where the buyer cries the goods are naught and then boasts of his bargain. Ellicott notices what is missing, that the parallel epistle adds a clause with nothing here to answer it, that we are members one of another — Barnes making the same observation from the other side, the reason there being fellowship and here the putting off of the old nature.

On the old and new man the grammarians are precise and the others doctrinal. Robertson distinguishes the two Greek words for new, the one here meaning young against the ancient man and the other, in the parallel epistle, fresh against the worn out, so that the sense is a continual refreshment of the young man in Christ; the verb for renewing seems coined for the purpose. Ellicott agrees that the new man here is properly the youthful man. Barnes argues from the parallel passage that since knowledge is added there to righteousness and true holiness, man before the fall had all three — the knowledge meant being of God. Clarke turns it on the heathen: ignorance was the grand characteristic of that state and knowledge of the Christian, and the injunction to know thyself was practicable only under Christianity. Calvin denies that a bare knowledge is meant and makes it the illumination of the Spirit, transforming the whole man.

Ellicott reads the list of abolished distinctions by what it adds and omits. The insertion of the barbarian and the Scythian, absent from the parallel elsewhere, rebukes the pride of intellect that lay at the root of the local error; the omission of male and female he explains by the different dangers of the two societies, the dignity of women needing assertion in one and the new freedom being apt to be abused into license in the other. Robertson calls it an ideal still far ahead of modern Christians, as the late war had proved. Barnes locates the Scythians geographically and Wesley calls them of all barbarians the most barbarous. Calvin says the clause draws the readers from ceremonies once more; the editorial matter printed with him tells of a Scythian at Athens who answered an insult by saying his country shamed him, but his accuser shamed his own. Cyril of Jerusalem gives the putting off its most vivid figure, bidding a former viper’s brood shed the slough of its old life as a serpent rubs off the old skin and grows young again.
12:
The clothing figure carries straight over. Robertson reads the imperative as the application of the new man under the image of the new garment, and Gill lists what is put on: not a robe of righteousness, which they had already, but conversation garments, adorning to themselves and to the doctrine they professed, without which they would walk naked — and, like Joseph’s, a coat of many colours. Henry says only that those holy towards God should be lowly and loving towards all men.

On the title elect of God the expositors differ in aim rather than sense. Ellicott takes it of the whole Church, election to privilege, coincident with the calling rather than opposed to it; and he finds the epithets holy and beloved laid down to prepare the two exhortations that follow, love one another because beloved, give thanks because holy. Robertson notes the Gospels keep a distinction between called and chosen where Paul keeps none. Clarke turns it polemically: the apostle’s design was to show God had chosen the Gentiles to be as truly his people as the Jews ever were, so he gives them the old name. Wesley states the order plainly, holiness being the consequence of election. Calvin makes the list the effects and evidences of renovation, and reads the clause as a condition: God has sanctified you and received you into his love on these terms, that ye be merciful.

Clarke alone presses the metaphor into more than metaphor. Granting the phrase figurative, he suspects a higher meaning — as the clothes are put over the body, so the tenderest feeling should always be within reach of the miserable, at hand, feeling and commiserating as soon as touched. He adds that almost every important manuscript reads the singular for the received plural, with scarcely any change of sense. Calvin distinguishes the graces: gentleness is chiefly in look and speech, while what follows it reaches also to the inward disposition.

Forgiveness produces the one open disagreement. Barnes resolves it into four duties — harbour no malice, do good as though no offence were given, say we forgive when asked, and treat the man ever after as if he had not injured us — and finds three properties in the pattern: Christ forgave freely, entirely and for ever. Clarke enters a caveat: no man should harbour ill will for a moment, but the offended party is not called actually to forgive until the offender acknowledges the fault, since Christ himself does not forgive us till we return confessing. Robertson observes the word for the grievance occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and that the second participle takes the reflexive pronoun where the first took the reciprocal. Ellicott notes the manuscripts favour Lord over Christ, with no real difference. Henry is content to observe that quarrels arise even among the elect, instancing the sharp contention that parted Paul and Barnabas.

The bond of perfectness draws the sharpest comment. Ellicott thinks the phrase was suggested by the perfection the local teachers claimed: they sought it in a knowledge peculiar to the few, the apostle in a love open to all. Clarke reports a rival reading, unity for perfectness, in several manuscripts and the Old Latin, and makes love the girdle binding the rest of the clothing. Barnes says the other graces without it would leave a painful want of harmony, and that neither faith nor zeal nor prophecy nor the tongue of angels would answer instead. Calvin turns on those who argue from the verse that love justifies: the apostle describes not how men are made perfect before God but how they may live perfectly among themselves — and in any case perfect love is nowhere to be found. Henry lays the foundation in faith and the top-stone in charity; Wesley says the love of God contains the whole of Christian perfection and connects all its parts.
15:
The first words are disputed and the verdict unanimous. Gill reports the Latin, Syriac and Ethiopic versions and the Alexandrian copy reading the peace of Christ; Clarke notes that on this evidence Griesbach admitted it into his text; Ellicott says flatly that the true reading is Christ and the received one borrowed from Philippians; Robertson simply prints it so. Ellicott makes the verse the hinge, joining the love of man before to the thankful service of God after.

On the verb the expositors agree and Wesley does not. Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Calvin all take it from the games: the umpire who presides and awards the prize. Gill has him award the victory and the crown; Barnes borrows from Doddridge the phrase sit as umpire, the soul being liable to agitation like a multitude and needing something to preside over it; Robertson notes the verb occurs here alone in the New Testament; and Calvin turns it to the wrestler who carries off the palm, making peace a bridle on the affections that hurry us into quarrels and secret grudges. Clarke draws a test: when a man loses his peace it is an awful proof he has lost something else. Wesley alone reads the word as reward rather than umpire, making the peace the recompense of preceding love and obedience. On the thankfulness following, Calvin prefers be amiable, sweetness of manners rather than remembrance of favours, while Barnes observes that an ungrateful people is commonly a tumultuous one.

The indwelling word draws out the two most personal comments here. Calvin uses it against those who in his own day interdict the people from the Scriptures and cry that no pestilence is more to be dreaded than throwing the reading open to the common people: the apostle addresses men and women of all ranks, and would have them not merely taste but advance every day. Chrysostom commits the same reading to the married and worldly, arguing that where the rich in money is impoverished by his fines, the man rich in doctrine spends nothing when he bears what he would not choose. Wesley notes that calling all Scripture the word of Christ asserts the divinity of the Master; Robertson, that the phrase occurs nowhere else and means in you, not among you; Clarke hears an allusion to the Shechinah, quoting the rabbinic maxim that wherever the Law is, the Presence is with it.

Where the sentence divides is genuinely open. Clarke says bad pointing has made the verse scarcely intelligible and that the original absolutely requires his arrangement, carrying in all wisdom forward to the teaching. Ellicott reaches the same division by the symmetry of the original, teaching in wisdom answering singing in grace, against the English version. Robertson answers that either punctuation makes good sense, the older manuscripts having none at all.

Barnes and Ellicott independently make the same large claim for hymns. Barnes recalls the saying that whoever makes a nation’s ballads need not care who makes its laws, and holds it truer that whoever makes a church’s hymns moulds its sentiments more than those who preach or frame its creeds. Ellicott says that for good and for evil the hymns of the Church have largely influenced her theology. Clarke turns the same interest into complaint, calling what is commonly sung a congeries of unmeaning sounds in which melody is sacrificed to a harmony destroying the simplicity of worship. On the closing rule Clarke digresses to the Mohammedans, who prefix the name of God to every book, even one he judges abominable. Ellicott hears in the household code that follows the presence of Onesimus, the runaway slave, behind the emphasis on masters and servants. Cyril of Jerusalem is present only by catchword, citing the parallel command to sing among his proofs that the Spirit subsists, and showing from Exodus that the Lord proclaimed the name of the Lord.
18:
Chrysostom asks why these household rules appear only here and in three other letters, and answers that there were probably dissensions in these cities; he settles on the guess that this church was by now well grounded, so the rules come in as a finishing. Three of the fullest expositors decline to comment at all. Gill refers the reader to his own note elsewhere, Barnes gives only the parallel verse numbers, and Clarke says the directions are so exactly the same in substance that repetition is needless.

Calvin, adding only what is peculiar here, raises a question of construction. Some read, be subject in the Lord, as it is fit; Calvin takes it the other way, as it is fit in the Lord, meaning by the Lord’s appointment, so that the subjection rests on the authority of God rather than on propriety. Ellicott too sends the reader to the other epistle. Robertson notes the word for own, genuine there, is absent here, and that the article marks off class from class. He and Wesley independently hear a military term in the verb, Wesley likening it to the submission soldiers pay their general; and Robertson cautions that wives have rights, the assumption being that the husband has a head, and a wise one. Henry grounds it on the order of creation, Adam first formed and Eve deceived, and adds that the submission is not to a tyrant. Calvin makes the answering command a guard against that, authority being in danger of turning tyrannical.

On the husband’s besetting fault the comments are short and sharp. Clarke says wherever bitterness is, love is wanting, and where love is wanting in married life there is hell upon earth. Ellicott corrects it to grow not bitter, suffer not yourselves to be exasperated, and notes the word is used figuratively here alone. Robertson reads both imperatives as habits, keep on loving and stop being bitter, calls this the sin of husbands, and says the bitter word rankles in the soul. Wesley adds that bitterness may exist without appearance of anger.

The command to children raises the hard case, and Calvin and Cyril of Jerusalem meet it by different roads. Calvin asks what is to be done if parents order something unlawful, and answers that the qualification in the parallel epistle must be understood here; the word all shows that obedience is owed not merely to just commands but to unreasonable ones, since many comply only where the thing is not grievous. He lays down three duties — to refuse nothing however disagreeable, to defer in indifferent things to the station parents hold, and not to argue as equals — conscience always excepted. Cyril of Jerusalem reaches it through a saying of Christ: not that whoever loves father or mother is unworthy, but whoever loves them more; only when earthly fathers are of a contrary mind to the Father in heaven is the word disobeyed. Robertson notes the hard part is that the obedience is continual, not occasional, and blames waves of lawlessness on children never taught it.

The last verse turns on a reading. Ellicott holds that provoke not to anger was borrowed from the parallel epistle and that the true text says provoke not to emulation — the thing forbidden being a constant restless stimulation, the spurring of a willing horse, ending in failure and despondency. Robertson keeps the ordinary sense, the verb occurring twice only, in a good sense elsewhere and here meaning to nag as a habit. On the result all agree. Barnes distinguishes flattery from encouragement and describes the man who is never satisfied breaking his child’s spirit until the child gives over trying and grows sullen and indifferent. Robertson points to runaway children and even child suicides, Wesley says such children turn desperate or stupid, and Henry warns that holding the reins too tight makes them fly out with greater fierceness.
22:
Gill defines the extent of the obedience first: in all things relating to the body and not the conscience, worldly and not spiritual, within a master’s power and lawful to command, and even in what is difficult and disagreeable. Robertson observes the word is really lords, and that these Christian slaves had Christ for lord and were still to obey lords in the flesh; he adds that the compound rendered eye-service is a coinage of the apostle, found only here and in the parallel and afterwards only in Christian writers, that men-pleasers is another late compound, and that singleness of heart comes from a word meaning without folds. Wesley glosses eye-service as being more diligent under the eye than at other times. Barnes, as through the whole household code, supplies only cross-references.

Gill raises a question of scope that the others do not. Some have thought the next verses address the Colossians generally and all good works whatever; but from the connection with what precedes and with the opening of the next chapter he confines them to servants. On working heartily, Robertson notes the parallel adds with good will by way of explanation, and calls doing it as to the Lord the highest test of service, adding that he wishes it were always true. Wesley turns it into a motive: men-pleasers are soon dejected and made angry, while the single-hearted are never disappointed, because they have another aim which the good or ill treatment of those they serve cannot touch.

The promised reward puts two of them to the same difficulty. Gill grants it is called a reward because the apostle is speaking to servants and uses language agreeable to them, enjoyed when the work is over as a servant takes his wages at evening; but it is not given for working, and is received not as a reward of debt but of grace. Calvin reaches the same place by another road: the very thing bestowed in reward of works is freely given, since the inheritance comes of adoption. Calvin also finds consolation in the earlier clause, that while servants willingly serve their masters their service is acceptable to Christ as though rendered to him. Clarke puts it plainly to men who own nothing — here you have neither lands nor property, but an inheritance is in store. Robertson notes the word for the recompense means the full paying back and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and suggests the closing clause may be an imperative, keep on serving.

Who the wrongdoer is at the last verse divides them three ways. Ellicott says he is clearly the master, citing the parallel, while granting that the phrase cannot be limited to him. Robertson says it is not clear, that it holds of either, and reports one commentator taking it of both; he calls it a general law of life, fair and square. Calvin reads it wholly of the master: if servants are oppressed by unjust cruelty God will take vengeance and will not overlook the injury on the ground that they are slaves, and he adds the pastoral reason for saying so, that servants often try to avenge cruel treatment themselves and must be taught to wait for the judgment of God. Clarke and Gill read it the other way. Clarke observes that an unfaithful servant may defraud his master in many ways without detection, that wasting a master’s goods is such a wrong as God will resent, and that God alone is the defence against him; Gill allows both, listing embezzlement on the one side and withheld wages and hard blows on the other. On the closing words Clarke says God neither esteems nor despises any man for his outward condition, every man being in God’s eye what he is in his soul, and Robertson that there is respect of persons with men but not with God.
